newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INTERVIEW-Advantage to launch radio EFTPOS.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Advantage to launch radio EFTPOS.

text.p: Advantage Group Ltd Chief Executive Clive Cooper-Smith said on Monday that the small technology firm expects to have radio frequency EFTPOS terminals available in New Zealand and Australia by early 1997.
Cooper-Smith told Reuters in an interview the terminals would allow normal EFTPOS (electronic funds transfer at point-of-sale) transactions without conventional phone lines.
Advantage supplies the hardware, software and network systems for around 65-70 percent of New Zealand's EFTPOS terminals and around 20 percent of Australia's.

"I think we are on the back straight in terms of the traditional terminal that sits on a shop counter," Cooper-Smith said. "We have not even begun with the next range, which will be radio frequency terminals," he said.
Bellsouth expected to make the service available through its GSM network, as did Telecom Corp of NZ.

"It's the next stage, and then we've got to go back and make all those terminals that are out there now capable of handling things like Mondex (a stored value smart card)," he said. Mondex is due for release in the next 18-24 months.

Cooper-Smith said there were obvious applications for the Advantage Solo for people on the move, such as taxi drivers, but there were uses for stores who like to change their counters around every season.
Advantage also expected to introduce EFTPOS debit technology into Australian and New Zealand households in 1997.
A major EFTPOS helpdesk contract was also in the wings.

There was still significant growth to come out of the Australian market in traditional EFTPOS terminals and Australia also had potential to take up add-on services, such as help desks and loyalty programmes.
Advantage decided a year ago that it could not sustain its future purely on selling terminals.

"There were a lot of other things that we really didn't separate or focus on. We just bundled it into the terminal and sold a terminal and looked at it as a terminal sale instead of the special software that we wrote for people to accept their own private label cards, like (discount retailer) The Warehouse."

That led to Advantage splitting into two divisions -- Advantage Communications Technologies, which puts product out into the market, and Advantage Systems, which offers the full range of "upstream and downstream" services.
Cooper-Smith said he was looking closely at Advantage's ability to develop software for terminal manufacturers in international markets and licence the software to them.
